The dazzling, seductive, and turbulent reign of King Charles II, England's 'Merry Monarch'. Surviving nine years of poverty-stricken continental exile following the execution of his father and hiding in the Boscobel Oak, Charles returned in 1660 amid hysterical rejoicing to restore the English monarchy. Reopening theaters, championing the Royal Society alongside Isaac Newton and Christopher Wren, Charles's court was an explosion of hedonistic glamour, populated by mistresses like Nell Gwyn and Barbara Palmer. Navigating the horrors of the Great Plague of 1665 and leading firefighting efforts during the Great Fire of 1666, Charles outmaneuvered the Whigs during the Exclusion Crisis to preserve Stuart rule. Discover the Merry Monarch.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, our Kings and Queens of England series examines the ultimate royal survivor: an exiled prince who returned to dance through the ruins of Puritanism, save his capital from apocalyptic flame, and forge modern London: King Charles II. Here is George with the grand saga of the Merry Monarch.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE OAK TREE AND CONTINENTAL EXILE: 1630 TO 1660
Born in May 1630 at St. James's Palace, Charles Stuart was a tall, swarthy prince whose dark southern complexion inherited from his French mother, Henrietta Maria, earned him the affectionate family nickname 'the Black Boy'. Thrust into civil war at age twelve, Charles commanded royal armies in the West Country before escaping to Jersey and France. In 1651, following his father's execution, twenty-one-year-old Charles formed a desperate alliance with Scottish Covenanters, being crowned King of Scots at Scone before leading an army into England. Crushed by Cromwell at the Battle of Worcester, Charles spent forty-four days as a hunted fugitive with a thousand-pound price on his head. Disguised as a woodcutter in coarse homespun clothes with his dark curls cut short, Charles spent an entire day hiding in the thick foliage of the Royal Oak at Boscobel Wood while Roundhead soldiers searched beneath. For nine long years, Charles lived in threadbare continental exile in Paris, Cologne, and Bruges, dependent on meager pensions, developing a cynical, charming pragmatism and an iron determination never to set out on his travels again. During his forty-four days on the run following the catastrophic defeat at Worcester, Charles demonstrated incredible physical resilience and acting genius. Disguised as 'William Jackson', a tenant's son in greasy leather breeches, Charles rode a horse carrying the gentlewoman Jane Lane pillion behind him through Roundhead checkpoints. When a blacksmith in Warwickshire shod his horse and remarked that Charles Stuart ought to be hanged, the disguised king cheerfully agreed that the rogue deserved a hanging if caught. The memory of the humble commoners—Catholic priests, servants, and woodsmen—who risked their lives to shelter him without ever betraying him for the thousand-pound reward fostered in Charles a lifelong gratitude and an enduring disdain for self-righteous puritan grandees.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE RESTORATION: THE RIDING INTO LONDON: MAY 29, 1660
When Oliver Cromwell died and the Commonwealth collapsed into military anarchy, General George Monck marched his army from Scotland to London, recalling the Long Parliament and inviting Charles to return. From Breda in the Netherlands, Charles issued the Declaration of Breda, promising a general pardon for all past offenses, payment of army arrears, and liberty for tender consciences. On his thirtieth birthday, May 29, 1660, King Charles II made his triumphant royal entry into London along a route seven miles long. The reception was an explosion of national ecstasy: the roads were strewn with flowers, wine flowed freely from public street conduits, and citizens wept with joy after eleven years of dour Puritan rule. Diarist John Evelyn recorded: 'I stood in the Strand and beheld it, and blessed God; and all this without one drop of blood spilt.' With characteristic witty self-deprecation, Charles remarked to his courtiers that it must have been his own fault that he had stayed away so long, for he had met with nobody today who did not protest he had always wished for his restoration. The Declaration of Breda was an exquisite triumph of political moderation drafted by Charles and his wise advisor Edward Hyde, Earl of Clarendon. By promising an indemnity to all former rebels except those whom Parliament specifically exempted—the regicides who had signed his father's death warrant—Charles prevented a vengeful, bloody civil backlash. The coronation at Westminster Abbey on St. George's Day, April 23, 1661, was celebrated with new royal regalia crafted to replace the ancient crown jewels melted down by Cromwell's Commonwealth, including St. Edward's Crown, the Orb, and the Sceptre, asserting the unbroken majestic lineage of the Stuart dynasty.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE MERRY MONARCH: NELL GWYN, BARBARA PALMER, AND THE ROYAL SOCIETY
Charles's court became a glittering, scandalous reaction against the joyless austerity of the Commonwealth. Theaters were reopened, with women permitted to perform on the English stage for the first time in history. Charles was an incorrigible womanizer, fathering at least fourteen illegitimate children by a succession of glamorous mistresses upon whom he bestowed peerages, palaces, and royal revenues: Barbara Palmer, Duchess of Cleveland; the French Catholic Louise de Kérouaille, Duchess of Portsmouth; and the witty, beloved Cockney orange-seller and actress Nell Gwyn, whom Charles called his 'pretty, witty Nell'. Yet beneath the court debauchery, Charles was an ardent, intelligent champion of modern science. In 1662, he granted a royal charter to the Royal Society of London, establishing the world's foremost scientific institution, bringing together luminaries like Robert Boyle, Robert Hooke, and Sir Isaac Newton. Charles maintained his own private chemical laboratory at Whitehall, taking a personal interest in navigation, clocks, and naval architecture. Charles's open, shameless patronage of his royal mistresses created a court of breathtaking theatrical indulgence. Barbara Palmer, created Duchess of Cleveland, demanded forty thousand pounds a year from royal revenues and lived in palatial luxury, while the Protestant actress Nell Gwyn won the hearts of ordinary Londoners. When a furious Protestant mob surrounded Nell's carriage in Oxford, mistaking her for the unpopular Catholic French mistress Louise de Kérouaille, Nell stuck her head out the window and laughingly shouted: 'Pray, good people, be civil; I am the Protestant whore!' The crowd cheered and let her pass. Concurrently, Charles founded the Royal Observatory at Greenwich in 1675, appointing John Flamsteed as the first Astronomer Royal to map the stars for naval navigation.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE GREAT PLAGUE OF LONDON: 1665
In the sweltering summer of 1665, an ancient, apocalyptic terror struck London: the bubonic plague. Carried by fleas on black rats, the pestilence swept through the crowded, timber-framed slums of the city with horrifying speed. Victims developed agonizing swollen buboes in their groins and armpits, vomiting black blood and dying within forty-eight hours. Red crosses were painted on the doors of infected houses with the chilling plea: 'Lord have mercy on us!' Watchmen guarded the doors from outside, trapping entire families to die together. At night, the death carts rattled through deserted, grass-grown cobblestones, the drivers ringing brass handbells and shouting: 'Bring out your dead!' The court and wealthy aristocrats fled to Oxford and Salisbury, leaving the brave Lord Mayor Sir John Lawrence and dedicated physicians to face the nightmare. Over one hundred thousand Londoners—nearly a quarter of the city's population—perished in six agonizing months, their bodies dumped into vast plague pits at Aldgate and Finsbury. Diarist Samuel Pepys recorded the creeping horror of the Great Plague of 1665 in London with chilling intimacy: noting the red crosses upon doors, the silence of the Thames, and the tragic sight of infants being pulled from the arms of dead mothers. Lord Mayor Sir John Lawrence remained heroically at his post in Guildhall, organizing food supplies and grave-digging crews as over seven thousand people died each week at the height of the summer heat. The pestilence finally subsided as autumn frosts arrived, having claimed over one hundred thousand souls and exposing the catastrophic vulnerability of medieval urban slums.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE GREAT FIRE OF LONDON: SEPTEMBER 1666
Barely had the plague subsided when a second biblical catastrophe struck. On the night of Sunday, September 2, 1666, a spark from an oven in Thomas Farriner's bakery on Pudding Lane ignited a fire. Fanned by a violent, unseasonal easterly gale and fed by pitch, tar, and brandy in Thames-side warehouses, the flames raged for four terrifying days. Charles II and his brother James, Duke of York, displayed magnificent physical courage: taking personal command of the firefighting efforts, the King rode through the burning streets with buckets of water and bags of gold coins, handing money to exhausted laborers, ordering houses blown up with gunpowder to create firebreaks. The fire incinerated eighty-seven parish churches, forty-four guild halls, thirteen thousand houses, and the colossal medieval Gothic cathedral of Old St. Paul's, whose lead roof melted and poured down Ludgate Hill like molten rivers. Miraculously, fewer than twenty people were officially recorded dead. From the smoking ashes, Charles commissioned Sir Christopher Wren to design fifty-one magnificent churches and the iconic classical masterpiece of St. Paul's Cathedral, resurrecting London in brick and Portland stone. During the Great Fire of 1666, King Charles II and his brother James personally labored for thirty hours alongside common London citizens, passing leather water buckets and supervising the demolition of buildings with gunpowder to create firebreaks. John Evelyn described the sky of London as an incandescent dome of flame two miles broad, so bright that a letter could be read at midnight ten miles away in Highgate. When Old St. Paul's Cathedral caught fire, the ancient wooden scaffolding surrounding it erupted into a blazing inferno; the colossal stone vaults collapsed into the crypt, crushing centuries of tombs and libraries in an apocalyptic avalanche of fire and stone.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE POPISH PLOT AND THE EXCLUSION CRISIS: 1678 TO 1681
The political sunset of Charles's reign was dominated by anti-Catholic paranoia. Charles's Portuguese queen, Catherine of Braganza, was barren, leaving the royal succession to the king's openly Roman Catholic younger brother, James, Duke of York. In 1678, an unprincipled charlatan and defrocked Anglican clergyman named Titus Oates concocted the 'Popish Plot'—a fictional Jesuit conspiracy to assassinate King Charles, massacre Protestants, and place James on the throne. Anti-Catholic hysteria swept the nation: Parliament passed the Test Act barring Catholics from office, and twenty-two innocent Catholic priests and peers were executed on Oates's perjured testimony. Led by the Earl of Shaftesbury, a new political faction known as the Whigs attempted to pass the Exclusion Bill to bar James from the throne, proposing Charles's handsome Protestant bastard son, the Duke of Monmouth, as heir. Charles demonstrated consummate political mastery: refusing to disinherit his legitimate brother, Charles dissolved successive parliaments, received secret French subsidies from Louis XIV that made him financially independent, and rallied conservative Tory loyalists to crush the Whig opposition without shedding a drop of blood. The Popish Plot was a masterpiece of mass hysteria manufactured by Titus Oates, an expelled Anglican clergyman of repulsive appearance and morals. Oates claimed that the Queen's physician, Sir George Wakeman, planned to poison the King while French troops landed in Ireland. When magistrate Sir Edmund Berry Godfrey was found murdered on Primrose Hill shortly after interviewing Oates, London descended into manic terror: MPs wore armor to Parliament, and citizens carried pocket daggers for fear of papist massacres. Charles personally interrogated Oates in council and caught him in blatant lies, yet was forced to sign execution warrants for innocent Catholic peers to prevent an armed uprising by Shaftesbury's Green Ribbon Club.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: DEATHBED CONVERSION AND THE LEGACY OF THE KING: FEBRUARY 1685
On Monday morning, February 2, 1685, while being shaved in his bedchamber at Whitehall Palace, fifty-four-year-old King Charles II suddenly let out a loud cry, rolled his eyes, and collapsed into a violent apoplectic convulsion. Royal physicians subjected the dying monarch to agonizing seventeenth-century medical tortures: bleeding sixteen ounces from his arm, applying blistering plasters to his shaved head, and administering enemas and antimony emetics. Throughout his prolonged four-day agony, Charles maintained his exquisite, gentle courtly wit: apologizing to his weeping courtiers for being 'such an unconscionable time dying'. On the evening of February 5, his brother James smuggled a Catholic priest, Father John Huddleston—who had helped save Charles at Boscobel thirty-four years earlier—into the bedchamber. Charles formally reconciled with the Catholic Church, receiving the last rites in absolute secret. In his final whispered words, he urged James to care for his mistresses, murmuring: 'Let not poor Nelly starve.' On February 6, 1685, the Merry Monarch died peacefully. He was buried in Henry VII's chapel at Westminster Abbey, having saved the monarchy through unmatched charm, pragmatism, and political genius. In his final years, Charles governed without a parliament, having secured secret annual subsidies of one hundred thousand pounds from his cousin King Louis XIV of France under the secret Treaty of Dover. He outmaneuvered the Whigs with consummate patience, watching the radical opposition collapse into treason in the Rye House Plot of 1683, which aimed to assassinate Charles and James on their return from Newmarket races. When Charles suffered his fatal stroke in February 1685, he passed the crown to his brother in absolute security, leaving behind a nation prosperous, culturally vibrant, and at peace, remembered forever as the charismatic Merry Monarch.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Thank you for joining us for this episode of Most Fascinating Stories. If you enjoyed this chapter of Charles II: The Merry Monarch, the Restoration, the Great Fire, and the Plague, subscribe to the show, share it with a fellow history lover, and tune in next Tuesday for our next journey into history's most extraordinary events. Until next time, I'm Rebecca.
